p: Massa' is the heading of a prophecy of judgment, and its root means to lift.
b: The Hebrew massa' comes from nasa', "lift," so it is a "lifting up" of the voice, or a load the prophet carries. The KJV has "burden." Jeremiah plays on both senses and forbids the word as a slogan (Jeremiah 23:33-40). Nahum 1:1, Zechariah 9:1 and Malachi 1:1 open the same way, and Isaiah uses it for the oracles against the nations (Isaiah 13:1). Habakkuk's oracle is odd: most of it is a conversation in which the prophet is the one who speaks up. The word still fits, since the load he carries is what he has seen. This Plain English Translation uses "oracle" every time, as in Proverbs 30:1.

p: The book gives no father, town or date; the legends about him come much later.
b: Habakkuk is named only here and at 3:1. The book gives no father, hometown or king. The name may come from a Hebrew root meaning "embrace" or from an Akkadian plant name; neither is certain. Later stories fill the gap. Bel and the Dragon (a Greek addition to Daniel, in the Catholic and Orthodox Bibles) has an angel carry Habakkuk by the hair from Judea to Babylon with a meal for Daniel in the lions' den. The Lives of the Prophets, a Jewish work of uncertain date, gives him a tribe and a hometown. These are legends, not evidence. The book itself shows a man who knows the temple songs and the old poems of God's march from the south (chapter 3).

t: "How long?" the prayer of the hurt
p: The cry that opens many psalms, and the cry Jeremiah and Job raise against God.
b: "How long?" is the standard opening of a lament in the Psalms: Psalm 13:1-2; Psalm 94:3. Jeremiah brought a case against God in the same spirit (Jeremiah 12:1), and Job cried "Violence!" and got no answer (Job 19:7). Habakkuk says it at the start of his book, so the book begins with a believer accusing God of deafness. The accusation is not dropped at the end. It is answered, then raised again (1:12-17), then carried to the watchtower (2:1). The Bible's own prayer book allows this. The martyrs under the altar ask the same question at Revelation 6:10.

p: The book's key word: wrong done by force, mostly to those who cannot hit back.
b: Chamas is injury done by force, with no regard for law. It is the sin that filled the earth before the flood (Genesis 6:11). Habakkuk uses it at 1:2, 1:3 and 1:9, and then in the woes at 2:8 and 2:17, so the word frames the whole book: the cry for help at the beginning, the verdict on the oppressor near the end. The same word is used for what Judah's own powerful do (Jeremiah 22:17) and for what the Chaldeans do (1:9). Habakkuk never says the second kind is better than the first. Each time the Plain English Translation uses "violence."

a: Why do you show me wickedness
p: Moses, Jeremiah and Job also say that God is the one who lets the wrong stand.
b: The sentence turns the usual prophetic charge around. Prophets normally say that the people see wrong and do nothing; Habakkuk says God shows him wrong and does nothing. Moses had said that God made things worse (Exodus 5:22-23), and Jeremiah that God had tricked him (Jeremiah 20:7). Jewish readers have drawn courage from it: the Talmud pictures Habakkuk standing his ground until God answers (Bavli Taanit 23a, on 2:1). The complaint is not a loss of faith: the man who says it is arguing with God and not leaving him, and the book keeps him in the room until the answer comes.

p: Torah here means the teaching that guides a society, which has stopped working.
b: Torah has a wide range. In the Law of Moses it is the body of laws, but the word means "teaching," and a priest's or a judge's ruling is also a torah. Here it is what should steer the community, and it has gone numb. The verb puag is used of Jacob's heart going numb with shock when he heard that Joseph was alive (Genesis 45:26). So the law is not repealed; it has stopped moving. Jeremiah complains the same way when the scribes' pen makes the law a lie (Jeremiah 8:8). In the Plain English Translation, torah is "law" when it is the covenant order, with "teaching" marked in the notes.

a: The wicked have the righteous surrounded
t: Who are the wicked, and who are the righteous?
p: Judah's own powerful men, foreign oppressors, or the Wicked Priest of Qumran: readers differ.
b: Habakkuk does not name them, and readers have disagreed. (1) Most modern commentators (Roberts, for one, is explicit) take 1:2-4 as Judah's own injustice, probably under Jehoiakim after Josiah's death; the words "law" and "justice" point to the courts, and the Chaldeans only arrive at 1:6. (2) Some place the book under Josiah and read the wicked as Assyrians or Egyptians. (3) Others hear a foreign power already at work and read 1:5-11 as a larger judgment on it. (4) The Qumran community's commentary on Habakkuk, Pesher Habakkuk, reads the wicked as the "Wicked Priest" and the righteous as its "Teacher of Righteousness." The Plain English Translation stays with the plain Hebrew: wicked and righteous inside one society.

p: The Habakkuk commentary from Qumran has "traitors" here and applies it to its enemies.
b: Pesher Habakkuk (1QpHab) is a Qumran scroll from the late first century BC. It quotes Habakkuk a line at a time and says, "This refers to ..." (the Hebrew pesher means "interpretation"). On this verse, as published by Horgan and others, the commentary reads "traitors" for "the nations" and applies the verse to those who sided with the "Man of the Lie" against the community's "Teacher of Righteousness." This is the community's reading, not the source of the Plain English Translation. The Greek "scoffers" below may come from the same Hebrew word (see the variant on this verse).

a: that you will not believe when it is told
p: Paul warns the synagogue in Pisidian Antioch with this verse, in its Greek form.
b: Paul ends his sermon in Pisidian Antioch with a warning from this verse: "See, you who sneer! Stand amazed, and vanish! / In your own days I am at work on a deed, / a deed you would never believe / if someone told you about it." (Acts 13:41). Paul follows the Greek, which has "scoffers" and "vanish" where the Hebrew has "among the nations" and a doubled "be astonished." The sense is the same warning: God is doing something no one would credit. In Habakkuk it is the Chaldean rise; in Acts it is the news about Jesus. Reading the Hebrew and the Greek side by side shows both uses.

p: The people of southern Babylonia whose dynasty ruled Babylon from 626 BC.
b: Kasdim, "the Chaldeans," were a people of southern Babylonia. Nabopolassar, a Chaldean, took the throne of Babylon in 626 BC, and his son Nebuchadnezzar finished the work. Babylon and Medes together destroyed Nineveh in 612. In 605 Nebuchadnezzar beat Egypt at Carchemish (Babylonian Chronicle), and from then on Judah lay in his path: Jehoiakim served him three years and then rebelled (2 Kings 24:1). "I am raising up" is the same sort of language Jeremiah uses of Nebuchadnezzar, "my servant" (Jeremiah 25:9). In the Plain English Translation, Kasdim is "the Chaldeans," as in 2 Kings 25. In Daniel the word can also mean a learned class.

p: Before 605, between 605 and 597, or after Alexander: the verse is the main evidence.
b: The verb is a participle, "I am about to raise," and the verse reads as if the Chaldeans are not yet at Judah's gate. Three dates are argued. (1) Before Carchemish (605 BC), under Josiah or just after: the rise of Babylon is the surprise of 1:5. (2) Between 605 and 597, under Jehoiakim: the most common view (for example Roberts), since the nation is already marching and Judah's courts are already corrupt. (3) A much later date: Bernhard Duhm (1906) proposed changing "Chaldeans" to "Kittim" and reading 1:5-11 as Alexander's Greeks. The Qumran commentary does read the Kittim here, but its Hebrew text says Chaldeans. Duhm's emendation has few followers.

p: The words echo the curse that God would bring a nation from far away against a disobedient Israel.
b: Deuteronomy warns that if Israel breaks the covenant the LORD "will raise up a nation against you" from far away, which "will dive on you the way an eagle swoops" (Deuteronomy 28:49). Habakkuk's nation "marches" far and "flies like an eagle" (1:8). The answer to the prophet's complaint is therefore not new: God is doing what the covenant said he would do to a people who broke its justice. That is one of the reasons many scholars think the first complaint is about Judah's own lawlessness. The prophet has asked for justice, and the justice is arriving in a form that shocks him.

a: Its justice and its grandeur come only from itself
t: A nation that is its own law
p: Mishpat is God's word for what the courts should keep; here it is a power's own rule.
b: Mishpat ("justice") is the central word of the book's first complaint (1:4), and here it returns with an ugly twist: this nation's "justice" is whatever comes out of itself. It admits no law above it. The partner word se'et ("grandeur," from "lift") sounds like massa' in 1:1. The Assyrian king likewise boasts in Isaiah that he did it by his own strength and wisdom (Isaiah 10:13). The line prepares for 1:11, where its own strength is its god. The Plain English Translation keeps "justice" so the reader hears the same word used for the courts, for God's judgment (1:12) and for this nation's will.

a: heaps up dirt and takes it
p: Ancient armies took walled towns by piling an earth ramp against the wall.
b: A siege ramp was packed earth, stone and timber built up against a wall until the attackers could walk up to the top. The Assyrians used ramps, and the great ramp at Lachish (about 701 BC) has been found; the Babylonians used them against Jerusalem (Jeremiah 32:24; Ezekiel 4:2). The line is a joke about the walls kings are proud of: a pile of dirt beats them. The Plain English Translation keeps the plain image; some translations use "siege ramp" or "mound," and the Hebrew is just "dirt."

a: sweeps on like the wind and moves past
t: Wind, spirit, or a change of mind?
p: The Hebrew ruach means wind or spirit, and the Greek reads a very different verse.
b: The Hebrew says something like "the wind (or spirit) swept on and passed over, and he is guilty." The word ruach can mean "wind," "spirit," or "mind." The Plain English Translation reads the nation as sweeping by like a gust, and then the text calls it guilty. The Septuagint reads it that way and ends with a different thought (see the variant). The Hebrew Masoretic Text has "guilty": the nation's attack is itself its crime. That fits the next clause, where the nation is guilty because its strength has taken the place of God.

a: whose own strength is his god
p: The nation worships its own power, which is why Habakkuk 1:16 has it offering to its net.
b: "His strength is his god" echoes Job's sneer at those who bring their god in their hand (Job 12:6) and the Assyrian king's boast (Isaiah 10:13-14). It is the heart of the charge against the Chaldeans: they do not simply break the law, they put their own force where God should be. It sets up the picture in 1:15-16 of the fisher who offers to his own net. The Qumran commentary reads this as the Kittim sacrificing to their military standards and bowing to their weapons.

a: are you not from ancient times
p: The prophet starts his second complaint by reminding God who he is.
b: The word qedem ("ancient times") is the language of the old songs about God as king before the world (Psalm 74:12; Deuteronomy 33:27). The prophet builds his protest on it: you are the Holy One from the beginning, so why do you make evil win now? The same word comes back at 3:6, "His ways are the ways of long ago." The pairing "my God, my Holy One" ('elohay qedoshi) shows the prophet speaking for himself. Each title, "Holy One" and "Rock" among them, is a way of holding God to his own character.

p: Tsur is God as a fixed place of safety; the verb hokiach means to correct or argue a case.
b: "Rock" is a common title for God in the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:4, 15, 18), a rock that does not move. The verb hokiach at the end of the verse means to "set right," the way a judge or a parent corrects. The prophet is thinking of the Chaldeans as God's instrument for that purpose, as Isaiah says of Assyria, "the rod of my anger" (Isaiah 10:5). It is a strange sort of correction, and the next verse says why he cannot accept it: the one he uses is guiltier than the ones he corrects. The Plain English Translation deliberately renders the verb here as "correction" but the related noun tokhachat at 2:1 as "complaint," because there the sense is the prophet's own protest (see the note at 2:1); the two share a root, so the prophet's protest answers the "correcting" God has just announced.

a: Pure are your eyes, so you cannot see evil
p: God's purity is not blindness: the prophet asks why he looks on the treacherous.
b: The line is often quoted to say that God cannot look at sin. The Hebrew is tehor 'enayim mere'ot ra', "pure of eyes from seeing evil." The min ("from") before "seeing" carries the sense "too pure to," and the Plain English Translation's "so you cannot see evil" is a sense line for it. The prophet's point is an argument, not a doctrine of blindness: if God's eyes cannot approve evil, why does he "gaze" (nabat) at the treacherous in the next line and stay silent? The tension is the book's theme, and it echoes Abraham's question, "Will the judge of all the earth not do what is just?" (Genesis 18:25), and Jeremiah's, "Why does the way of the wicked go well?" (Jeremiah 12:1).

p: Bogedim, "the treacherous," is the Hebrew word the Greek and the Qumran commentary read at 1:5.
b: Bogedim is a heavy word in Hebrew: people who betray a covenant, a marriage, a king. It is used of the powerful who do violence to the weak in Isaiah (Isaiah 21:2; 24:16). The Qumran commentary on this verse names the "House of Absalom" and the men of their council who kept silent when the Teacher of Righteousness was reproved. In 2:5 the same root is used of wine as a traitor. That repeated word is part of why some think that Greek "scoffers" in 1:5 stands for the Hebrew "traitors."

a: You have made human beings like the fish of the sea
p: Genesis 1:26 gave humans rule over the fish; here humans are the fish.
b: In Genesis humans are made to rule over "the fish of the sea" and the crawling things (Genesis 1:26-28). Here people are "like the fish of the sea" with no one to rule over them. The creation order has been turned over: people are caught like animals, and God is the one who "made" them so. The picture belongs to a long line of prophetic fishing scenes, in which captives are hauled up with hooks (Amos 4:2; Jeremiah 16:16; Ezekiel 29:4). Ezekiel turns the picture on Pharaoh, a monster in the water who is himself hooked (Ezekiel 29:3-4).

p: He worships what he uses to catch: his own methods and weapons.
b: A fisher gives thanks to his net because it is the source of his food. The image says that the conqueror's own tools have become his god (1:11). Ancient armies did carry standards and weapons as sacred objects. The Qumran commentary applies the line to the Kittim, who "sacrifice to their standards and worship their weapons of war." The Bible sees the same fault in anyone who trusts the work of his own hands (Isaiah 44:9-20; Deuteronomy 8:17-18). Habakkuk ends the section with the question whether he can go on forever (1:17).

p: Lo yachmol, "he will not spare," ends the first section with the question the prophet cannot let go.
b: The Hebrew verb chamal means to spare, to take pity. It is what the Chaldeans do not do, and what the prophet implies God has not done by letting them. The first section of the book closes with a question and no answer. The answer will not come here; it comes from the watchtower in chapter 2. The question "Will he go on emptying his net?" asks whether the successful violence will ever be stopped, and the later woes say it will (2:6-8).
orig: לֹא יַחְמוֹל (lo yachmol), 'he will not spare'

a: I will stand at my post
p: Prophets are lookouts; the Talmud says a rainmaker drew a circle in imitation of this verse.
b: A watchman on a tower is one of the prophets' pictures of their own work (Isaiah 21:6-8; Ezekiel 3:17; Jeremiah 6:17). Habakkuk does not watch for an enemy but for God's reply. The Talmud tells of Honi the Circle-Drawer, who stood inside a circle and refused to leave until God sent rain, and it cites Habakkuk's "I will stand at my post" as the model (Bavli Taanit 23a). The picture shows how Jewish readers took the verse: a man who will not be moved away from a question until he is answered. Compare Micah 7:7, where the prophet says he will watch for the LORD.

p: The Hebrew tokhachti can mean the charge I bring, or the rebuke I receive.
b: The noun comes from the verb hokiach of 1:12. It can mean the charge a person brings in a lawsuit ("my complaint"), or the correction a person is given ("my reproof"). The Greek reads the second ("my reproof"). The Plain English Translation takes "my complaint" because the prophet has just been the plaintiff (1:2-4; 1:12-17), and the question is what he will answer when God answers. Either way the point is the same: the prophet knows that his own speech is on trial too.

t: The Qumran commentary: the Teacher of Righteousness
p: The Habakkuk commentary says God told Habakkuk what would come, but not when; the Teacher received the rest.
b: Pesher Habakkuk reads this as follows (in the translation by Vermes): God told Habakkuk to write what would happen to the last generation, but did not tell him when the age would end. The "one who reads" is then the Teacher of Righteousness, to whom God made known all the mysteries of the prophets' words. So the community took Habakkuk as a code that only their founder could crack. This is the Qumran community's reading of the verse, not the Plain English Translation's. In the community's reading, the interpretation of the vision was given to the Teacher alone.

a: make it clear on the tablets
p: Public tablets were posted so passers-by could read a notice; Isaiah also wrote on a tablet for later.
b: The tablets here are writing boards, probably of wood or clay or stone, posted in a public place. Isaiah was told to write on a large tablet and on a scroll so that it would stand "for a later day" (Isaiah 8:1; Isaiah 30:8). The command makes the vision a public notice, not a private secret. It also explains what follows: if the vision is written, it can be checked later against what happened, and Deuteronomy gives that very test for a true prophet (Deuteronomy 18:21-22).

p: The verb "run" can mean to read in a hurry, to carry the message, or to live by it.
b: The phrase is literally "so that he may run, one who reads in it." Three readings are argued. (1) The writing is so large and clear that someone running past can read it. (2) The reader takes the message and runs with it, as a herald does. (3) "Run" means to pursue it, as the Greek says: "so that the one who reads it may pursue it." Many English versions take the second. The Plain English Translation keeps the verb "run" and leaves the purpose open.

p: Yafe'ach means to pant or blow: the vision strains toward its end like a runner.
b: The verb yafe'ach means to puff or pant, and the picture is of the vision racing toward its goal. The Greek has "it will rise" (as if from yafia', "shine"), and "the end" can mean the end of the age or just the fixed end of the matter. The next phrase, "it will not lie," turns the picture to speech: unlike the false vision that people sell (Jeremiah 14:14), this one will not deceive. "Wait for it" is the Hebrew chakkeh lo, a word of patience that comes back at the close of the book in the prophet's own waiting (3:16).

p: The Greek makes the vision a person, "the coming one," which Hebrews applies to Christ.
b: The Hebrew says of the vision, "it will surely come." The Septuagint turns the sentence around: "if he is late, wait for him, because the coming one will come." Hebrews 10:37 uses that form for Christ: in this Plain English Translation's rendering from the Greek, "For in a very short time, the One who is coming will come, and will not be late." The Talmud also reads this verse of a person: it warns against calculating the end, because those who say the time has passed give up waiting; instead one should wait as the verse says (Bavli Sanhedrin 97b). Hebrews then adds 2:4 in the Greek order (this Plain English Translation's rendering from the Greek): "And my righteous one will live by faith; but if he draws back, my soul takes no pleasure in him," and goes on, "We are not those who draw back to destruction, but those of faith." There the verse is a pastoral call to endure, not a statement about justification.

p: The Hebrew 'uppelah is found nowhere else, and the Greek reads the line very differently.
b: 'Uppelah occurs only here. It is usually linked to the root 'pl, "swell," or to 'opel, "swelling, hill" (Isaiah 32:14), so a swollen, puffed-up person. The two Hebrew scrolls that preserve it (see the variant) have the same consonants. The Greek instead has "if he shrinks back," and Hebrews 10:38 uses the Greek. The line needs a person, and the Hebrew gives none: "it is swollen, his soul is not upright." The Plain English Translation adds "the one who" to make a subject, which most translations do.

a: the righteous will live by his faithfulness
p: The commentary applies the second half of the verse to those who obey the Law and trust the Teacher.
b: Pesher Habakkuk (1QpHab) quotes the line with be'emunato, "by his faithfulness," in its lemma, but its comment reads 'emunatam, "their faithfulness," and applies it to all who do the Law in the house of Judah, whom God will rescue from the judgment "because of their toil and their faithfulness to the Teacher of Righteousness" (in Vermes's translation). The commentary therefore reads the verse as loyalty to a person and obedience to the Law together. This is the community's reading. It is the oldest known Jewish commentary on the verse, and it shows that "faithfulness" was heard as loyalty to the Teacher there.

p: The rabbis say the prophets reduced Moses' 613 commandments until Habakkuk set them on one.
b: Rabbi Simlai taught that Moses was given 613 commandments. David reduced them to eleven (Psalm 15), Isaiah to six (Isaiah 33:15-16), Micah to three (Micah 6:8), Isaiah again to two (Isaiah 56:1), and Amos to one: "Seek me and live" (Amos 5:4). Then Habakkuk "came and based them on one": "the righteous will live by his faithfulness" (Bavli Makkot 23b-24a). The Talmud does not make faithfulness a replacement for the commandments. It treats it as the root the 613 grow from. Paul also takes this verse as central, in Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11, though he uses it differently; the Talmud text is centuries later, and the two are independent.

p: 'Emunah is steadiness, being reliable; it is the word Paul's Greek pistis translates.
b: 'Emunah comes from the root of "amen" and means being firm, reliable, true. It describes Moses' hands, which "stayed steady" until sunset (Exodus 17:12), and God's own faithfulness (Lamentations 3:23). So the Hebrew is not first about believing a doctrine but about being steady under pressure. Paul and the Greek writers use pistis, whose range is wider: trust, belief, and faithfulness. This Plain English Translation gives the Hebrew its own word, "faithfulness," and the Greek of Romans "faith." The difference is why readers still argue whether Habakkuk 2:4 was about trusting God or being loyal to him. Most scholars hold both senses live together.

p: Paul quotes the Greek form, without "his" or "my," for righteousness by faith.
b: Paul uses the verse twice. In Romans 1:17 he writes, in this site's Plain English Translation, "In it God's righteousness is revealed, from faith to faith, as it is written: 'The righteous will live by faith.'" In Galatians 3:11 (this Plain English Translation's rendering from the Greek) he argues that no one is justified before God by the law, because "the righteous will live by faith." Paul drops both "his" (Hebrew) and "my" (Greek), which leaves it open whose faith is meant. Two further disputes follow. Some, such as Cranfield, take "by faith" with "the righteous" ("the one who is righteous by faith will live"); most take it with "live." Richard Hays has argued that "the Righteous One" can be a title of Christ, so that the verse speaks of his faithfulness. Both are views, not settled results. The question is often put as the debate over pistis Christou, "faith of Christ" or "faith in Christ," in Paul's letters, and Hays's suggestion belongs to the same debate. The Orthodox Church's Old Testament is the Septuagint, so in its own Bible the line reads "my faithfulness."

t: The Qumran commentary: the Wicked Priest
p: The commentary applies the greedy, arrogant man to a priest who betrayed his early calling for wealth.
b: Pesher Habakkuk says this concerns the "Wicked Priest," who was called by the name of truth when he first took office, but when he ruled over Israel his heart grew proud, he abandoned God and betrayed the commandments for the sake of wealth (translated by Vermes). The commentary also changes one word of the text (see the variant). The Wicked Priest is never named, and scholars have proposed Jonathan, Simon, Alexander Jannaeus, and others from the Hasmonean house. The identification is open.

a: He opens his throat wide as Sheol
p: The mouth that never fills is Sheol's, the place of the dead that never says "enough."
b: Sheol, the realm of the dead, "enlarges its throat" in Isaiah (Isaiah 5:14), and in Proverbs Sheol and death are never satisfied (Proverbs 27:20; Proverbs 30:15-16). Habakkuk gives the same appetite to the conqueror: he takes in nations as Sheol takes in the dead. The verse links back to "swallows up" in 1:13. Wine is the first image of weakness ("a traitor"), and the throat is the second. Both say that the conqueror is ruled by what he thinks he rules.

p: Hoy is a funeral cry. Five woes follow, as a taunt song against the plunderer.
b: Hoy was the cry of mourners at a burial ("Oh, my brother!" in 1 Kings 13:30). Prophets use it as a funeral call over the living: this person is already dead. Habakkuk has five woes (2:6, 9, 12, 15, 19), in the pattern Isaiah uses for his six (Isaiah 5:8-23). The word is "Woe to" in the Plain English Translation every time it names the one addressed. Verse 6 calls the five a "saying" (mashal) and "a mocking song" (melitsah): the victims themselves sing it, like the song over the king of Babylon in Isaiah 14:4.

p: The Hebrew 'avtit is found only here; the guesses range from loans to a heavy load of mud.
b: 'Avtit occurs only here. The older Jewish and Christian tradition takes it as 'avot ("pledge"), the thing a lender holds, with the sense that the plunderer loads himself with debts. A pun has also been proposed: 'av "heavy" and tit "clay," a heavy load of mud. The Greek has a "heavy collar" (a yoke around his neck). Either way the picture is of a man who piles up what is not his and is dragged down by it. The Plain English Translation's "pledges" follows the first reading.

p: The Hebrew noshekha is from the verb "to bite" and also the word for interest.
b: The Hebrew word is literally "your biters" (noshekha), from nashak, "bite." The same root gives neshek, "interest," which the Law forbids charging a fellow Israelite (Deuteronomy 23:19-20). So the pun is the point: the creditor bites. The creditors are the many nations the plunderer has robbed, and they wake up and call in the debt. The Plain English Translation says "lenders" and keeps the bite in the note.

p: Babylon on most readings, but Jehoiakim, Assyria and Qumran's Wicked Priest have been named.
b: The woes name no one. Most commentators read them as aimed at Babylon, since the "nations" and "peoples" of 2:5 and 2:8 are the ones Babylon conquered (compare Jeremiah 50-51, where the same ideas turn on Babylon). A second reading finds a Judean king in the woes of 2:9-12; Jeremiah's own "woe" against Jehoiakim, who builds his house with unjust labor, is close (Jeremiah 22:13-17). Assyria has been proposed by those who date the book early. The Qumran commentary reads the woes of 2:5-17 against the Wicked Priest. The Plain English Translation leaves the plunderer unnamed.

a: the violence done to the land, to the town, and to all who live in it
p: The refrain of 2:8 and 2:17 can mean Judah and Jerusalem, or the whole earth.
b: The same line closes the first and the fourth woe (2:8; 2:17). "The land" ('erets) and "the town" (qiryah) can be the earth and its cities in general. They can also be Judah and Jerusalem, so that the violence done to "the land" is Babylon's work in Judah. Some commentators take "the town" to be Jerusalem in particular. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew words and does not choose.

p: A nest on a cliff is the image of a man who thinks nothing can reach him.
b: An eagle's nest on a cliff is the picture of safety. Obadiah uses it of Edom (Obadiah 4), and Jeremiah of Edom again (Jeremiah 49:16), and Balaam uses a nest in a cliff for the Kenites (Numbers 24:21). The woe accuses the one who gets rich unjustly to build a house out of reach of "harm" (ra'). Compare the tower of Babel (Genesis 11:4): a house made by wrong, lifted to be safe. The woe says it will cry out against him (2:11).

a: you sin against your own life
p: Nefesh means life, self or throat; wrongdoing hurts the doer.
b: Nefesh is the person's whole self, translated "soul" in older versions and "life" or "self" in newer ones. The idea that sin harms the sinner's own nefesh is in Proverbs (Proverbs 8:36; Proverbs 20:2). In context the plunderer ends peoples, and in doing so ends himself. The word comes back at 2:5, where his nefesh (throat) is as wide as Sheol.

a: the stone in the wall cries out
p: Blood cries out from the ground in Genesis 4:10; here the building itself accuses.
b: The house built by wrong becomes a witness against its builder. The idea is like Abel's blood crying from the ground (Genesis 4:10) and Job's wish that the earth not cover his blood (Job 16:18). Luke 19:40 has Jesus say that if the crowd were silent, the stones would cry out; many readers hear Habakkuk behind it, though the Gospel does not quote this verse. The Hebrew word for the beam, kafis, appears only here, and the Greek has "beetle," which is a reading of that rare word.

a: puts up a city with bloodshed
p: Micah says of Jerusalem's leaders that they build Zion with blood; Nahum calls Nineveh the city of blood.
b: The line is close to Micah 3:10, where Zion's leaders "build Zion with blood." Jeremiah's "woe" against the man who builds his house without righteousness stands behind it too (Jeremiah 22:13). Nahum 3:1 names Nineveh "the city of blood." The woe can be read of Babylon, which Nebuchadnezzar rebuilt with the labor of captives, or of Jerusalem under Jehoiakim, who used the labor of his people. Both fit, and the prophet may have left the picture open on purpose.

p: The line also appears in Jeremiah's long oracle against Babylon.
b: Jeremiah 51:58 says that Babylon's wide walls will be razed and that "peoples labor for emptiness, / nations for the fire, / and they wear themselves out." The same words appear in Habakkuk in a different order. One may have used the other, or both may quote a proverb about work that ends in fire. Either way, Habakkuk puts the wasted labor of the nations under the LORD of Armies' own hand: it is not an accident of history but his answer to the violence. The title YHWH tseva'ot is "the LORD of Armies" in the Plain English Translation throughout.

a: knowing the glory of the LORD
p: Habakkuk adds "glory" to Isaiah's line and changes the image of the water.
b: Isaiah 11:9 says, in this site's Plain English Translation, "knowing the LORD will fill the earth like waters covering the sea." Habakkuk's version adds "the glory of" and puts the verb in the passive. Numbers 14:21 has the promise as an oath: "the LORD's glory will fill all the earth." Habakkuk joins the two. The line is the book's answer to the cries of chapter 1: in the end the violence will not cover the earth; the knowledge of God's glory will. It stands in the middle of the woes, as a promise. The Greek has "it will cover them," a small change.

p: The Hebrew is shaky; the sentence slides from "his neighbor" to "your anger."
b: The line switches from the third person ("his neighbor") to the second ("your anger"), and the word for "pouring out" is rare. Both oddities show that the Hebrew was already a puzzle to the copyists. Wine and anger go together here: the host who gets his guests drunk and then looks at them (Genesis 9:20-27 has Noah's nakedness, seen by his son Ham). The Plain English Translation keeps the shift in person so that the reader can feel the prophet stepping from description to accusation. A variant gives "his anger," and the Greek has a completely different line.

a: The cup from the LORD's right hand
t: The cup of the LORD's anger
p: In the prophets, God hands a cup to the nations and they drink and fall.
b: The cup that goes around the nations is a prophetic image: God hands it, and they stagger (Jeremiah 25:15-29; Isaiah 51:17, 22). Lamentations 4:21 tells Edom that the cup is coming around to her too, and that she will get drunk and expose herself. Habakkuk joins that cup to the nakedness of 2:15: the one who made his neighbor drink and exposed him now drinks and is exposed. Jesus' cup in Gethsemane is often read as this cup taken by himself (Matthew 26:39), and Revelation 14:10 speaks of the wine of God's anger, poured into the cup of his wrath, which the worshippers of the beast drink.

p: Babylon cut Lebanon's cedars; the line may also mean the temple, called "Lebanon."
b: Lebanon's cedars were the great timber of the ancient world. Nebuchadnezzar's own inscriptions boast that he cut them for his buildings, so the line may refer to the felling of the forests and the killing of their animals. Jeremiah uses Lebanon for the royal house of Judah (Jeremiah 22:6-7, 23), and later Jewish tradition often reads "Lebanon" as the temple (as with Zechariah 11:1 in the Talmud, Yoma 39b). The woe can therefore mean the damage to the forests, to the temple, or to both. The Plain English Translation says "Lebanon" and leaves the choice open.

p: The Bible's mockery of idols is told here almost the same as in Isaiah 44 and Jeremiah 10.
b: The idol is a "teacher of lies": it claims to speak and it cannot. Isaiah 44:9-20 describes the carpenter who burns half a log for warmth and carves the rest into a god. Jeremiah 10:3-5, 14-15 calls idols like a scarecrow in a cucumber field. Psalm 115:4-7 says they have mouths and do not speak. The Hebrew 'elilim is "worthless gods" in the Plain English Translation throughout, and the pun with 'elohim is intended. The woe fits the book: the conqueror trusts in his net (1:16), in his strength (1:11), and in his images (2:18).

p: Elijah mocked Baal's prophets with the same call; Psalm 44:23 turns it on God.
b: On Mount Carmel, Elijah told Baal's prophets to shout louder because Baal might be asleep (1 Kings 18:27). Here the idol-maker says "Wake up!" to wood. The Psalms use the same verb for the people's cry to God: "Get up! Why do you sleep, Lord? / Wake up!" (Psalm 44:23). The difference is that the LORD is awake and answers (2:2). The command to the idol is the sign of its emptiness: it needs a human voice to rouse it, and cannot answer.

a: Hush before him, all the earth!
p: The same command appears in Zephaniah and Zechariah as a call before the day of the LORD.
b: After the mute idols (2:18-19), the earth is told to hush before the God who is present. Zephaniah 1:7 uses the same verb of the coming day of the LORD, and Zechariah 2:13 of the LORD rising from his holy dwelling. "His holy temple" can be the Jerusalem temple or the heavenly one (Psalm 11:4). In the Diaspora the haftarah for the second day of Shavuot is Habakkuk 3 (Bavli Megillah 31a); some communities begin the reading at this verse, others at 3:1. The Greek has "let all the earth be reverent." The old hymn "Let all mortal flesh keep silence" (from the Liturgy of St James) is often heard as a later echo of this verse and Zechariah 2:13.

a: A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet
t: Is chapter 3 part of the book?
p: The chapter is in the Greek and in two Hebrew scrolls but not in the Qumran commentary.
b: Chapter 3 has its own heading, three selah marks and a closing note for the music director, like a psalm. It is in the Septuagint, and the printout of the Dead Sea data shows Hebrew text of it in the Murabba'at scroll of the Twelve (Mur88). The Qumran commentary stops at 2:20 and does not interpret chapter 3. Some scholars (Albright and Cross among them) judged the poem to be much older than the rest of the book, perhaps a hymn from the early monarchy; Hiebert's study is a leading defense of its antiquity. Others read the whole book as one design, with the prayer as its answer to the dialogue. Jewish and Christian worship have used it as a unit for centuries.

p: A musical or poetic term, plural of the shiggaion in Psalm 7; its meaning is lost.
b: Shiggayon heads Psalm 7, and shigionoth is its plural. The meaning is not known. The word may come from shagah, "to wander, reel," and so be a wild or ecstatic song; or it may be a term borrowed from the Akkadian word for a lament. The Greek translator took it as "with a song." The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew word and the note, as it does for other technical words ("Selah" at 3:3, 9, 13, and "the music director" at 3:19).

t: Habakkuk 3 in Jewish and Christian worship
p: A reading for the second day of Shavuot, a canticle in the Greek Odes, and a Holy Saturday text.
b: The poem is the haftarah for the second day of Shavuot (Pentecost) in the Diaspora, when it recalls the LORD's coming from Sinai (see Deuteronomy 33:2); the Talmud already names the reading (Bavli Megillah 31a), and some communities begin it at 2:20, others at 3:1. In Greek manuscripts the poem is Ode 4 of the biblical canticles sung at morning prayer, and the Byzantine rite sings it at Matins. In the Roman rite it was a canticle of Lauds on Fridays. In each use the verses about the LORD's march, the shaking of the mountains and the final joy were heard as the church's own hymn.

p: Shim'akha is the report of God's deeds, the story of the exodus.
b: The Hebrew noun shema' means a report, what is heard. It is the word for what the nations heard of the exodus, and trembled at (Exodus 15:14). Job uses the verb to say that he had heard of God but now sees him (Job 42:5). So the prophet's fear is the fear of someone who has heard the old stories of what God did, and prays that God will do it again. The Plain English Translation reads "what is told of you" to keep the sense of a story passed on.

p: A hard phrase: in the middle of time, or at the turn of the years. The Greek has "two living things."
b: Beqerev shanim means "in the midst of years." Readers take it in several ways: in the middle of the years of our lives, in the present time between the old acts of God and the coming ones, or in the middle of the years of the exile. The verb chayyehu ("give it life") makes God's "work" something that can die and needs reviving. The Septuagint reads the words as "in the middle of two living things." The Old Latin followed the Greek (in medio duorum animalium), while Jerome's Vulgate has in medio annorum, "in the midst of the years." Christians and Christians later joined the "two animals" to the ox and the donkey of Isaiah 1:3 at the Nativity (the Hebrew has no animals). The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.

t: Compassion in the midst of wrath
p: The prayer asks God to keep the Exodus 34 balance even in judgment.
b: "In anger, remember compassion" asks that God's anger, which the chapter is about to describe, not swallow his mercy. The pairing is the creed of Exodus 34:6-7, in which the LORD is "compassionate and gracious" and also punishes. The prophet asks that the first not be lost in the second. The word is rachem, "compassion" (from rechem, "womb"), as in Isaiah 54:7-8, where God's anger is only for a moment. The Plain English Translation keeps "compassion" for rachamim, as in the other books of the Twelve.

t: The LORD comes from the south
p: Teman, Paran and Sinai were the places an old poem pictured the divine warrior setting out from.
b: Four old poems put the LORD's march in the south: Deuteronomy 33:2 (Sinai, Seir, Paran), Judges 5:4-5 (Seir, the field of Edom), Psalm 68:7-8 and here. Teman was in Edom (Amos 1:12; Jeremiah 49:7) and Paran was the desert south of Judah. The poem sees the LORD arrive from there at the head of his armies. Frank Cross and others grouped these poems as some of the oldest Hebrew verse, and this hymn is often taken as one of them. The word for God here, 'eloah, is a rare singular form used mostly in poems.

p: A mark in the Psalms whose meaning is unknown, probably musical.
b: Selah occurs seventy-one times in the Psalms and three times in this chapter (3:3, 9, 13). Its meaning is lost. Ancient translators took it as "forever" (Jerome's Latin has "always") or as a musical sign for a pause, a raised voice or an instrument's interlude. The Greek translates it with diapsalma, which suggests an interlude. In this Plain English Translation the word is kept at the end of the line without translation, and the note says it is a technical sign. In chapter 3 it falls at the three points where the poem turns.

p: Qeren means a horn and also a ray of light; Moses' face "shone" with the same root.
b: The Hebrew qeren means "horn," and the dual qarnayim is "two horns." It can also mean a ray, as in the verb said of Moses' face when he came down Sinai (Exodus 34:29-35). Jerome's Latin mistook that verb as "horned," which gave rise to the horned Moses in medieval art. In Habakkuk the context is light ("brightness like the light"), so "rays" is the best guess. The Greek has "horns in his hands." The next line says the strength is "hidden" there, as if the light were the visible edge of a power kept in reserve.

p: Resheph was a plague god in Canaan and Egypt; Habakkuk makes him the LORD's attendant.
b: Deber is "plague," the killing sickness of Exodus 9 and Deuteronomy 32:24. Resheph is the name of a god of plague and fever in Canaanite and Egyptian texts. Here, as in Deuteronomy 32:24 and Psalm 78:48, the word is only a force that obeys the LORD: it walks in front of him and behind. The Bible uses the old names of such powers while taking away their divinity. The Greek reads "word" for deber (the same consonants), and the Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew pointing.

p: The Hebrew consonants can be read as "he measured the earth" or "he shook it."
b: The Masoretic pointing reads the verb as "he measured" (from madad). The Latin has "he stood and measured the earth." Many scholars read the same consonants as a different verb, "he shook" (mud), because the next lines have the nations jumping and the mountains breaking. The Greek says "the earth was shaken." The Plain English Translation takes "shakes" and notes the alternative in the variant. If "measured" is right, the picture is of God as surveyor, laying out the land he gives.

a: His ways are the ways of long ago
p: A rabbinic play turns "his ways" into "laws" and promises the world to come.
b: The Hebrew halikhot 'olam lo means "his ways are from long ago." The rabbis read halikhot as halakhot, "laws," and taught: "Whoever studies halakhot every day is promised that he is a child of the world to come, as it is said, 'halikhot olam lo,' do not read halikhot but halakhot" (Bavli Megillah 28b; Niddah 73a). It is a play on the letters, not a claim about the original meaning. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew sense: God's ways are old, unchanged since the exodus.

p: Two southern peoples that tremble as the LORD comes from Teman.
b: Midian lay in the northwest of Arabia, east of the Gulf of Aqaba; it was the land where Moses lived and of Jethro (Exodus 2:15-22), and the Midianites were Gideon's enemies (Judges 7). "Cushan" is found only here, and it is probably a form of Cush, a name used for peoples of the south, in Nubia or in Arabia; Moses had a Cushite wife (Numbers 12:1), and the verse sets Cushan and Midian side by side as one southern region. Another man with a similar name, Cushan-rishathaim, is a king in Judges 3:8-10, but there is no sign of a link. The Greek reads "the tents of the Ethiopians."

a: Was it against the rivers, LORD, that you burned?
p: In Canaanite poems the storm god fights Sea and River; in the Bible God does, without a rival.
b: In Canaanite texts from Ugarit, the storm god Baal fights Prince Sea and Judge River. Hebrew poems use the same names and pictures (Psalm 74:13-15; Psalm 93:3-4; Psalm 89:9-10). The questions here are asked in that language, but the answer is the exodus and the crossing of the Jordan, where the LORD parted real waters (Exodus 15; Joshua 3). Cross judged that the Bible has "historicized" the old battle; it keeps the vocabulary but gives it to a God without rivals. "Rescue" translates yeshu'ah, the word for victory and for salvation (3:13, 18).

p: The Hebrew shevu'ot matot omer has been read in at least four ways.
b: Shevu'ot matot 'omer is among the hardest lines in the Bible. Proposals include: (1) "oaths are sworn on the arrows (matot as "shafts"): a word"; (2) "the oaths to the tribes (matot "tribes") are your word," which is what the Latin translates; (3) other proposals that change the pointing or the letters; (4) the Greek, "you stretch your bow upon the scepters, says the LORD." The Plain English Translation takes (1) as the nearest to the printed text; the third line is clear: the LORD cuts the earth with rivers.

t: The sun and moon stood still
p: Joshua 10 has the same verb; here the sun and moon freeze before the LORD's lightning.
b: The verb 'amad, "stand," is the one Joshua 10:12-13 uses when the sun and moon stand over Gibeon and Aijalon. Here, though, the lights stop because the LORD's arrows and spear flash brighter than they do. Ancient Near Eastern art shows sun and moon stepping aside before a storm god. Some readers link the verse to Joshua; others take it as the sky's reaction to a thunderstorm. The Greek reads "the sun was raised up, and the moon stood in its place."

p: To thresh is to trample grain on a floor; Israel is later told to thresh the mountains.
b: A threshing sledge crushes grain on a threshing floor. In the prophets it is the picture of conquest: Damascus is threshed with iron sledges (Amos 1:3), and Zion is told to rise and thresh the peoples (Micah 4:13). Habakkuk's use is the LORD's own action, in anger. The war does not end with defeating Babylon alone but with the nations as a whole, a larger scene than the book's first prophecy.

p: The king, the people, or the Messiah: the word is singular and the meaning is open.
b: Meshichekha is singular, "your anointed." Three readings are held. (1) The Davidic king of the poem's own day, since kings were anointed (Psalm 18:50; Psalm 89:38). (2) The whole people, as in Psalm 105:15 and perhaps Isaiah 45:1, where Cyrus is called anointed. (3) The Messiah, a reading the Greek (christon) and many Jewish and Christian writers adopted. The Latin differs: "to save with your anointed," taking 'et as "with." The Plain English Translation keeps the object marker and leaves the identity open.

a: gloating as if to eat the poor in a hiding place
p: The enemy is a hunter lying in wait for the weak, as in Psalm 10.
b: The picture of someone lying hidden in order to seize the poor appears in Psalm 10:8-10, where the wicked "sits in ambush" in villages and catches the afflicted in his net. Habakkuk has used the net before (1:15-17). The poem's message is that the hunters fall into their own spears: "with his own shafts you pierced the head of his warriors." The reversal is the same as in the woes: the plunderer is plundered. The Hebrew has an unusual note in the Leningrad Codex that the word "warriors" is written one way and read another (see the variant).

t: Claude's theory: the waiting is the answer
p: The prophet obeys 2:3 here: "wait for it" becomes "I will wait quietly."
b: Claude's theory. The book gives the prophet two commands: "wait for it" (2:3) and "hush before him" (2:20). Chapter 3 shows him doing both. He hears, shakes, and says "I will wait quietly for the day of trouble" (3:16). The verb anuach ("rest") is a different word from 2:3's chakkeh ("wait"), but both are about being still while the judgment goes on. On this reading the book does not solve the problem of 1:2-4 by explaining it; it gives the prophet a way to live inside it. Some commentators likewise treat the prayer as the book's answer; the reading of the two verbs is mine. I rest it on 2:3, 2:20 and 3:16.

p: The attacker of 3:16 may be Babylon, or a day still to come.
b: Yegudenu ("attacks us") is from a root meaning "to raid." The enemy is not named. If the poem is the prophet's response to the Chaldeans (1:6), the "day of trouble" is Babylon's campaign against Judah; if the poem is older, the enemy is any attacker. The Greek reads "to go up to the people of my sojourning," a different sense. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew. Either way the prophet decides to wait, and the verse after is the book's most famous act of trust.

a: Even if the fig tree never buds
p: The list is the covenant curses of Deuteronomy turned into a vow of joy.
b: Fig, vine, olive, field, flock and herd are the items in the Deuteronomic curses (Deuteronomy 28:38-42, 51) and in the famine descriptions of the prophets (Joel 1:10-12; Jeremiah 5:17; Hosea 2:12). The prophet takes the whole list of losses and says that he will rejoice anyway. The "even if" is therefore not a hypothetical drought but the covenant's last stage: everything the land can lose, lost. It is the opposite of Deuteronomy's promise, and the verse that follows is faith under the curse.

a: still I will exult in the LORD
p: Mary's song shares the closing words of the Greek of this verse.
b: The Greek of Habakkuk 3:18 reads "I will be glad in the Lord, I will rejoice in God my Savior." Mary's song ends with the same words: "and my spirit has found its gladness in God my Savior" (Luke 1:47). The Hebrew has "God of my salvation," which the Greek rendered "God my Savior." The echo is one of several in the Magnificat, which is stitched from Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2) and the Psalms. In Habakkuk, the joy comes after the harvest has failed; in Luke, it comes before the birth.

p: The same line is in David's song in 2 Samuel 22 and Psalm 18.
b: The line is also in David's song of rescue: "He makes my feet like a doe's" (2 Samuel 22:34; Psalm 18:33). The deer is surefooted on cliffs. "My high places" is a line from the old poems about the land (Deuteronomy 32:13; 33:29): the high ground of the land the LORD gave. Habakkuk takes a king's victory song and makes it the prophet's own. The Greek reads quite differently ("he will set my feet to a finish"). The prophet ends the book where the exiles will want to: on high ground and in song.

p: A psalm-style closing note: the poem was meant to be sung with strings.
b: "For the music director" (lamenatse'ach) heads fifty-five psalms, and "with stringed instruments" (binginot) heads several (Psalm 4; Psalm 6, and others). Here the note comes at the end instead of the front. "My" stringed instruments is odd: it suggests the prophet himself, or his guild, as the musician, or a later hand speaking in his voice. The note shows that the poem was used in worship, and that the book was meant to be sung as well as read.
